prompt: Why is the baseline built before the model rather than after it?
hint: Think about what the person building it already knows.

choices.text: Built after, it is chosen to lose
choices.why: Yes. Somebody who knows the model's score picks a bar it clears.

choices.text: Because scikit-learn fits dummies faster on an empty session
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Because a constant is the only kind of baseline that exists
choices.why: There are three kinds in the section, and the rule is the one that matters most here.

choices.text: So it can use the model's predictions
choices.why: A baseline that used the model would not be a baseline.

prompt: Match each baseline to what beating it proves.
hint: Each one rules out a simpler explanation for the model's score.

pairs.right: The model uses the features at all
It finds something an expert's sentence does not
Changing anything is worth the trouble

right_distractors: The model will work next year

prompt: Ana tries five rules and keeps the one that scored best on the months she reports as the test. What is wrong with her baseline?
hint: Choosing is learning.

choices.text: Rules must be scored with accuracy, not with net value
choices.why: A baseline is scored exactly like the model, and here that is net value.

choices.text: It has seen the test
choices.why: Yes. Its score is flattered exactly as an overfitted model's would be.

choices.text: Five rules is too few to find the one that a domain expert would actually have written
choices.why: More candidates chosen on the test would flatter it more, not less.

choices.text: Nothing: a rule has no parameters, so it cannot overfit
choices.why: Which rule to keep is a parameter, and it was set on the test.

prompt: Why do the credit's price and the split live in `feira.py` rather than in each program?
hint: What would two programs with slightly different splits produce?

choices.text: Python cannot import a constant defined in another file
choices.why: It can, and `from feira import CREDIT` is that.

choices.text: Because the files in `data/` are read-only
choices.why: They are not, and it would not matter.

choices.text: So every score is computed the same way, and comparable
choices.why: Yes. A different split in one program would change its score for a reason nobody sees.

choices.text: To make the programs run faster
choices.why: Importing a module saves no measurable time here.

prompt: `by_time` learns from every snapshot before July 2025 and tests on the ___ months from July to December.
hint: Count them.

prompt: `DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent")` scores 0.939 accuracy on the test months. What does that number mostly measure?
hint: It says *stays* for everybody.

choices.text: That the data is clean enough for a model
choices.why: Accuracy says nothing about cleanliness.

choices.text: How well the features separate leavers from stayers
choices.why: The dummy ignores the features completely.

choices.text: How rare cancellations are
choices.why: Yes. 93.9% of the test rows are people who stayed.

choices.text: How much money the credit made on the test months
choices.why: It sends no credit, so it made R$ 0.

prompt: The dummy says *stays* for all 24,257 test rows, and 1,484 of them cancelled. What is its accuracy, as a percentage with one decimal place?
hint: Right about everybody who stayed.

prompt: Match each `DummyClassifier` strategy to what it predicts.
hint: Only one of them is random.

pairs.right: The commonest class, with the class shares as probabilities
A class drawn at random in the training proportions

right_distractors: The class of the nearest training row

prompt: A credit costs R$ 40 and is worth 0.3 × 480 = R$ 144 when it reaches a leaver. Above what share of leavers among the people who get a credit does a policy start to make money? Answer as a proportion with three decimal places.
hint: Cost divided by what a hit is worth.

prompt: Subscribers with three or more skips cancel at several times the average rate, yet `skips_90d >= 3` loses R$ 32,280 on the training months. How can both be true?
hint: Compare the group's rate with the break-even point, not with the average.

choices.text: The rule was scored on the wrong months
choices.why: It was scored on the months it was chosen from, which flatters it if anything.

choices.text: Several times a small rate is still below 28%
choices.why: Yes. Most credits still land on people who were staying, and each one costs R$ 40.

choices.text: Skips are only recorded after the credit has already gone out
choices.why: `skips_90d` covers the 90 days before the snapshot.

choices.text: Net value penalises any rule that sends more than a thousand credits in a single month
choices.why: There is no such penalty; each credit is just priced.

prompt: The best rule made R$ 2,448 on the training months and lost R$ 576 on the test months. What is the most useful reading?
hint: It was the best of five on those months.

choices.text: The test months must contain an error
choices.why: Nothing suggests an error; a choice made on data often fails to travel.

choices.text: A rule that combines two conditions is always worse than one
choices.why: Nothing in the data says so; this one was simply chosen on too little.

choices.text: Some of its training score was luck
choices.why: Yes. The best of several candidates is partly the luckiest.

choices.text: The rule should be rechosen on the test months
choices.why: That would make the test a training set and its score worthless.

prompt: Why does lesson 2 use gradient boosting for its first model, without explaining it?
hint: Look at what `load_churn` leaves in the data.

choices.text: Because the baseline also uses it
choices.why: The baselines here use no model at all.

choices.text: It takes the data as it is
choices.why: Yes. Its algorithm is lesson 8; here it is a box.

choices.text: It is the only model that can beat a rule
choices.why: Several models in lessons 5 to 8 would beat this rule.

choices.text: It never overfits
choices.why: It can, and lesson 8 shows how to stop it.

prompt: The model sent 711 credits, 348 of them to people who were leaving. What share of its credits reached a leaver? Two decimal places.
hint: Hits over credits sent.

prompt: The model earns about 14% of what a perfect model would on the test months. What does that justify?
hint: A baseline and a ceiling answer different questions.

choices.text: Abandoning it, since 86% is left on the table
choices.why: It is still far better than anything simpler, which is the reason to have it.

choices.text: Lowering the ceiling
choices.why: The ceiling follows from the costs and the leavers; nobody sets it.

choices.text: Using it, with room above
choices.why: Yes. The baseline says it is worth having, the ceiling says how much better one could be.

choices.text: Claiming it is 86% wrong
choices.why: The 14% is a share of money, not of answers.

prompt: Why does `beaten.py` resample subscribers instead of rows?
hint: The same person appears up to six times in the test months.

choices.text: Subscribers are the target of the model
choices.why: The target is `churned`; the unit is a subscriber-month.

choices.text: Resampling rows would be too slow on 24,257 rows
choices.why: Rows would be faster, not slower.

choices.text: A person's rows rise and fall together, so treating them as independent makes the interval too narrow
choices.why: Yes. The interval would claim more certainty than the data holds.

choices.text: NumPy cannot resample a DataFrame by row
choices.why: It can, through positions, exactly as the program does with the subscribers' rows.

prompt: The 95% interval of *model minus rule* runs from about R$ 18,400 to R$ 25,900. Which reading is correct?
hint: The resamples come from these six months only.

choices.text: Next semester the model will make between those two amounts more than the rule
choices.why: Next semester is not a resample of this one; lesson 22 shows how it can differ.

choices.text: On data like this, the gap is far larger than the noise in measuring it
choices.why: Yes. That is all a test set can promise, and it is enough to decide.

choices.text: The model is 95% better than the rule
choices.why: 95% is the share of resamples inside the interval, not a size of improvement.

choices.text: There is a 95% chance the model is right about each subscriber
choices.why: The interval is about a difference in money, not about single predictions.

prompt: Two models differ by R$ 300 on the test months and the bootstrap interval of the difference crosses zero. What is the honest report?
hint: What can the test tell apart?

choices.text: Both models are useless
choices.why: Both may beat the baseline easily; they only tie with each other.

choices.text: Run the bootstrap again with another seed until it stops crossing zero
choices.why: That is searching for the answer you want.

choices.text: The better one by R$ 300 is the better model
choices.why: The interval says that order could easily flip with other subscribers.

choices.text: The test cannot tell them apart; choose on simplicity or cost
choices.why: Yes. A difference inside the noise is not a finding.

prompt: As a constant guess for delivery minutes, why does the median beat the mean on average absolute error?
hint: A few deliveries take an hour or two longer.

choices.text: The mean is computed with less precision
choices.why: Both are exact; the difference is what each minimises.

choices.text: Long outliers pull the mean up
choices.why: Yes. 11.6 against 12.0 minutes.

choices.text: The median uses the test months
choices.why: Both are computed on the training months only.

choices.text: The mean ignores the deliveries made in the rain
choices.why: It includes every delivery.

prompt: "Median minutes per km, times km" is off by 17.7 minutes, worse than any constant. What is missing from it?
hint: What does a delivery of 0.5 km still take time for?

choices.text: Enough training rows to estimate a median per kilometre
choices.why: 4,460 deliveries is plenty for one median.

choices.text: The city of the delivery
choices.why: The city median did no better than the overall one.

choices.text: A fixed part that does not grow with distance
choices.why: Yes. Loading the van and finding the door; lesson 5 fits a line with both parts.

choices.text: The rain
choices.why: Rain matters, but the hour-of-day median also ignores it and does better.

prompt: Of the five delivery baselines, what is the smallest average error, in minutes, that lesson 5's model has to beat?
hint: The median by hour of day.

prompt: Put the steps of an honest baseline comparison in order.
hint: Nothing is looked at on the test months until everything has been chosen.
items: Fix the split and the score
Choose the best rule on the training months
Fit the model on the training months
Score rule and model once on the test months

prompt: A colleague's new model scores 0.941 accuracy on the test months and they call it an improvement. What do you check first?
hint: What does the constant score on the same rows?

choices.text: How long it took to train
choices.why: Training time does not tell you if it beats the baseline.

choices.text: Whether 0.941 is above 0.9
choices.why: Any threshold picked out of the air says nothing about this data.

choices.text: Its net value, beside the 0.939 a constant scores
choices.why: Yes. Two tenths of a point above the dummy may be worth nothing at all.

choices.text: Whether it used gradient boosting or a simpler algorithm that is easier to explain
choices.why: The algorithm says nothing about whether the result is worth having.
